claims.claim: The British window tax was introduced in 1696 under King William III as a flat two-shilling house charge plus additional sums scaled to window counts.
claims.episode_span: Parliament had created the levy in 1696 precisely to gauge a household’s wealth from the outside without entering rooms.
claims.supporting_quote: In 1696, King William III of England, in dire need of additional revenues, introduced a dwelling unit tax determined by the number of windows in an abode.

claims.claim: After the 1797 rate increase, owners boarded up thousands of windows to lower their tax liability.
claims.episode_span: Lincoln Institute records show thousands of windows sealed after the 1797 rate increase alone.
claims.supporting_quote: In response, owners of dwellings attempted to reduce their tax bills by boarding up windows or by constructing houses with very few of them.

claims.claim: A physician reported that blocked windows in one dwelling removed all ventilation, allowed a fever to spread, and caused 52 deaths in the town.
claims.episode_span: A physician quoted by Guthrie in 1867 described one such house whose “overpowering and offensive” atmosphere became the source of a fatal fever that claimed fifty-two lives in the surrounding town.
claims.supporting_quote: it was propagated from it to other parts of town, and 52 of the inhabitants were killed

claims.claim: The window tax remained in force until its repeal in 1851.
claims.episode_span: Parliament received repeated petitions and finally repealed the tax in 1851.
claims.supporting_quote: The window tax was repealed in 1851
